steps.caption: At the start of a game the king has no move at all: every square around it holds one of White's own pieces.

line.say: A pawn steps out of the way. That frees the square e2.
Black makes a move of its own.
The bishop steps out and frees f1. The king has a square now, though it usually gets to safety by castling, which comes later. [I]

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
The piece on e1 is the white king.

steps.text: On a real board the king is rarely alone. Before it moves, ask three questions of each square around it. Is my own piece there? Is it next to the enemy king? Does an enemy piece attack it? A square that fails any question is crossed out. Why? One rule sits under all three: a move that leaves your king capturable is simply not allowed. Watch the questions on one board.

steps.caption: White to move. d3 holds White's own pawn. e4 and e5 touch the black king. The black pawn attacks d5. Four squares are left.

line.say: c4 is empty, far from the black king and attacked by nothing: it passes all three questions.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
The piece on d3 is White's own pawn.
One black piece (the pawn) attacks d5.
One black piece (the king) attacks e5.

steps.text: Why may a king never stand next to the enemy king? If it did, each king would attack the other, and each would leave itself capturable. So the squares between two kings are closed to both. The next board shows it.

steps.caption: The kings stand two files apart. f3, f4 and f5 touch both of them, so neither king may enter. Five squares are left for White.

line.say: The white king steps away from the gap and keeps its distance.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
The piece on e4 is the white king.

steps.text: Nobody will tell you which rule to use, so say the piece's name first, then use that piece's rule. On the next two boards the same square holds a king and then a knight. Everything else is the same, yet the squares differ. A king steps one square. A knight jumps in an L. Check the shape before you move.

steps.caption: The piece on e4 is a king. The black pawn attacks c5 and e5, so e5 is crossed out. The other seven neighbours are free.

line.say: d5 is straight in front of the black pawn, and a pawn attacks only diagonally, so it is safe.

claims.statement: The piece on e4 is the white king.
These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
The black pawn attacks e5.

steps.caption: Now the piece on e4 is a knight. It ignores its neighbours and jumps to eight different squares.

line.say: The knight jumps onto d6 and takes the pawn. A king could not have reached d6.

claims.statement: The piece on e4 is the white knight.
These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

steps.text: You met each kind of attacker alone in the last lesson. On a busy board they arrive together. Cross out squares one attacker at a time: the rook along its rank and file, the bishop along its diagonals, the knight by its jump, the pawn one step diagonally forward. A rook or bishop attacks only as far as the first piece in its way.

steps.caption: Four black pieces watch White's king on e4. The rook covers d3, e3 and f3. The bishop covers e3 and f4. The knight covers d4. The pawn covers d5. Only e5 and f5 remain.

line.say: e5 is attacked by none of the four pieces, so the king steps up the board.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
Only the rook attacks d3.
The rook and the bishop attack e3.
Only the knight attacks d4.
Only the pawn attacks d5.

steps.caption: The same position with a White pawn on c3. A line stops at the first piece in its way, so the pawn shelters d3 and f3 from the rook. Four squares are free now.

line.say: d3 is safe: the pawn on c3 blocks the rook's line along the third rank.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
Nothing attacks d3 once the pawn blocks the rook.
Nothing attacks f3 either.

steps.text: When a rook gives check, the king stands on the rook's line. Here is the trap: the square directly behind the king is attacked too, because the king would still be on that line after stepping back. The king does not shelter the square behind it. Study the board, then predict.

steps.caption: White is in check from the rook on e8. The king may not step up to e5, and it may not step back to e3 either. Six squares are left.

line.say: A step sideways leaves the rook's file, so the check is over.

claims.statement: White is in check from the rook.
These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
Stepping back along the line is illegal.
Stepping forward along the line is illegal.

steps.caption: A bishop gives check along a diagonal. The same idea holds: e5 is on the diagonal, and so is c3 behind the king. Both are crossed out.

line.say: Stepping off the diagonal ends the check.

claims.statement: White is in check from the bishop.
These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
Stepping back along the diagonal is illegal.
Stepping forward along the diagonal is illegal.

steps.text: A piece standing next to the king can be captured by the king, but only if it is not **defended**. A piece is defended when a friendly piece could take back on that square. Taking a defended piece would put the king on an attacked square, which is illegal. So ask: who else sees that square?

steps.caption: The black knight on e5 touches the king. Nothing black attacks e5, so the knight is undefended and the king may take it.

line.say: The king captures. It lands on a square no black piece attacks.

claims.statement: The king may capture on e5.
No black piece defends the knight.

steps.caption: Now a black pawn on d6 defends the knight. If the king took it, the pawn could take the king, so the capture is illegal.

line.say: The king settles for a safe step. Nothing attacks c3.

claims.statement: The king may not capture a defended piece.
One black piece (the pawn) defends the knight.
c3 is a legal step.

steps.caption: A defender can be far away. The rook on d8 looks down the open d-file at the knight, so it defends the knight from the other side of the board.

line.say: The king takes a safe step instead.

claims.statement: The king may not capture the defended knight.
The rook defends the knight.
e5 is a legal step.

steps.caption: Same position with a black pawn on d7. The pawn stands between the rook and the knight, so the rook no longer defends it. The king may take.

line.say: The king takes the knight. The pawn on d7 keeps the rook's line shut.

claims.statement: The king may capture on d5.
With the pawn in the way, nothing defends the knight.

steps.caption: Kings defend too. The black king on d6 defends the knight on d5, so White's king cannot take it.

line.say: A safe step instead.

steps.caption: A pinned piece still guards its squares. The rook on a8 pins the black bishop to its king, yet the bishop still attacks d5, so White's king may not take the knight.

steps.caption: The same rule works when the piece gives check. The queen on d5 attacks the king, but nothing defends her, so the king simply takes her.

line.say: The king captures the queen, and the check is over.

claims.statement: White is in check from the queen.
The king may capture the queen.
Nothing defends the queen.

steps.caption: Give the queen a defender, the pawn on c6, and the king cannot take her. It must step away: only c3 and e3 are safe.

line.say: Stepping aside ends the check.

claims.statement: White is in check.
The king may not capture the defended queen.

steps.text: A king in check has three answers: step away, capture the checker, or block the line. This lesson trains the first two. Blocking and pins get their own lessons later. [I]

steps.title: Defended or not
steps.prompt: Predict first. Each of the three positions differs from the first by exactly one piece. Which change matters for the king's squares, and which does not? Say why before you look.

steps.text: A far-away piece matters only if its line reaches the king's own square or a square the king could step to or capture on. A rook across the board can look frightening and change nothing. Emanuel Lasker (Common Sense in Chess, lectures 7 and 8, our summary of the sheet) counted the king's square and its eight neighbours when judging a mate. [I] Your checklist counts the same squares from the king's side.

steps.caption: The rook on a8 attacks only its own rank and file. It touches none of the king's neighbouring squares, so it changes nothing.

line.say: The king takes the knight. Nothing defends it.

The far rook does not defend the knight.
